content.title: About
content.content: Tomato soup in a can or carton is a ready‑to‑eat product made from ripe tomatoes, water, spices and a modest amount of salt. The reduced‑sodium version contains only 0.3 g of salt per 100 ml, making it suitable for people watching their sodium intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato soup is one of the most popular ready‑made soups worldwide.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that gives the soup its bright red color.
Canning preserves nutrients for 2‑3 years without the need for artificial preservatives.
Sodium reduction is often achieved by replacing part of the salt with potassium‑based salt substitutes.
Tomato soup is frequently used as a base for more complex dishes such as stews or sauces.

items.title: High in lycopene
items.content: Lycopene has antioxidant properties, supports heart health and may lower the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Reduced sodium
items.content: Lower salt content helps control blood pressure and reduces kidney strain.

items.title: Vitamins A and C
items.content: Tomatoes provide vitamins A and C, which support immunity and vision.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: A warm soup is easy on the stomach and promotes better nutrient absorption.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Being mostly water, the soup contributes to daily fluid intake.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or added spices.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Certain brands may contain added sugar, which should be considered in low‑sugar diets.

items.title: BPA in packaging
items.content: Carton packages can be lined with BPA‑containing resins; choose BPA‑free labeled products.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Although reduced, sodium is still present; people on strict low‑sodium diets should count it toward their daily limit.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the soup in a pot or microwave until boiling, optionally stir in fresh herbs, cream, or croutons. It can also serve as a base for pasta, risotto, or be added to vegetable stews.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can or carton in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for 3‑4 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

turkey-drumstick-cooked-skin-not-eaten.title: Turkey, drumstick, cooked, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a large bird native to North America. The drumstick is one of the most meaty parts, low in fat. When boiled without the skin, it retains protein and essential micronutrients while keeping calories low.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey meat is rich in tryptophan, an amino acid that supports serotonin production.
In the United States, turkey is strongly associated with Thanksgiving celebrations.
Drumsticks contain more iron than breast meat because of their denser muscle fibers.
Compared with chicken, turkey has a more pronounced flavor, making it popular in Asian cuisines.
The skin of turkey holds most of the fat, so it is often removed to reduce caloric content.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of cooked, skin‑less drumstick provides about 29 g of high‑quality protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Without skin, the fat content is under 2 g per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey supplies vitamin B6, niacin (B3) and riboflavin (B2), which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The drumstick provides iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation, immunity and bone health.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The high protein level helps maintain a feeling of fullness, beneficial for weight management.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked turkey may harbor pathogens such as Salmonella or Campylobacter. Proper cooking temperatures are essential.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to bird proteins, which can cause reactions ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Turkey is relatively high in purines, so people with gout should limit intake.

items.title: Sodium in processed versions
items.content: If the drumstick has been brined or marinated, sodium levels can be high, which is a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked, skin‑less drumstick can be diced for salads, added to soups and stews, or used in sandwiches. After boiling, a quick sauté gives a pleasant golden crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked turkey in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in sealed bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C before serving.
